newsitem.title: FINLAND: EMU woes cloud outlook for Finnish bonds - analysts.
newsitem.headline: EMU woes cloud outlook for Finnish bonds - analysts.

text.p: The risk of a delayed EMU start is weighing on Finnish bonds, although the anticipated U.S. rate hike on Tuesday removed some market tension and sent bond markets rallying, analysts said on Wednesday.

The Finnish 10-year yield gap over Germany has widened by 20 basis points to 57 in just two weeks, as non-core markets have suffered from talk of a delayed start of economic and monetary union, and it may rise to 70 or 80 basis points if this uncertainty prevails, they said.
"The Finnish/German yield spread is a difficult question now and we are likely to experience more peaks this spring due to EMU uncertainties," said OKOBANK treasury economist Teppo Koivisto.

He estimated that a worst case scenario could up the Finnish/German yield gap to 80 basis points which would be level with Denmark which has opted to remain outside the third stage of EMU and lagged other markets.

Business cycles in Europe remain different than in the U.S., where the Federal Reserve on Tuesday said it lifted its key federal funds rate by a quarter point to 5.50 percent to prevent inflationary imbalances, economists say.
Monetary policy tightening in Europe is highly unlikely in the next six months or even this year, analysts said.
"The markets need not fear any monetary policy tightening this year, as long as inflation remains subdued," said Jukka Lepomaki, chief analyst at Merita Bank.

Although the average of Finland's prominent forecasters estimates for gross domestic product growth is a brisk 3.8 percent for this year and 3.5 percent next year, all inflation forecasts put it below the Bank of Finland's target to keep core inflation at no higher than around two percent in the long run.

"Europe has a different economic cycle than the U.S. and particularly in Germany, there are no rate hike pressures," said Koivisto, adding that countries aspiring to join EMU were likely to conduct a uniform monetary policy with Germany.
In Finland, the only domestic risk is the round of wage talks for next year due to start in the autumn, analysts said.

If union's pay rise demands seem excessive, the Bank of Finland may opt to raise its key tender rate from 3.00 percent as a warning, much as it did in June 1995 when it last raised rates, analysts said.

So far, trade unions and employers have pledged to help keep inflation in check and the government has suggested that moderate wage hikes may be rewarded with income tax cuts, but the Finnish labour market is known to be unpredictable.

One worry is that the influential paper workers union has threatened not to join a comprehensive pay deal. Due to the union's bargaining strength, paper workers have historically often reached excessive pay rises and caused pressure for higher lifts in other sectors too, labour market experts say.
